claim: ChIP-MS analysis revealed 289 proteins that associate directly or indirectly with SOX18.
source: ChIP-MS analysis revealed 289 proteins, representing a variety of gene ontology (GO) classes of molecular function, that associate directly or indirectly with SOX18 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-MS analysis as stated in the text and referenced in Figure 1B.

claim: SOX18 interacts with itself and forms pairwise interactions with DDX1, DDX17, ILF3, STAT1, TRIM28, and XRCC5.
source: Using ALPHA-Screen, we observed that SOX18 interacts with itself, and also forms pairwise interactions with DDX1, DDX17, ILF3, STAT1, TRIM28, and XRCC5 (Figure 1C, left column '+', Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data as stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sm4 significantly disrupted 6 out of the 12 validated SOX18 interactions.
source: We found that Sm4 significantly disrupted 6 out of the 12 validated SOX18 interactions (Figure 1C, right column), with IC50 values ranging from 3.3 mM for SOX18-SOX18 to 65.9 MM for SOX18-RBPJ dimers (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Sm4's effect on SOX18 interactions with specific IC50 values.

claim: The IC50 for Sm4 disruption of SOX18-SOX18 interaction is 3.3 μM.
source: We found that Sm4 significantly disrupted 6 out of the 12 validated SOX18 interactions (Figure 1C, right column), with IC50 values ranging from 3.3 mM for SOX18-SOX18 to 65.9 MM for SOX18-RBPJ dimers (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the specific IC50 value for SOX18-SOX18 interaction disruption.

claim: The IC50 for Sm4 disruption of SOX18-RBPJ interaction is 65.9 μM.
source: We found that Sm4 significantly disrupted 6 out of the 12 validated SOX18 interactions (Figure 1C, right column), with IC50 values ranging from 3.3 mM for SOX18-SOX18 to 65.9 MM for SOX18-RBPJ dimers (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the specific IC50 value for SOX18-RBPJ interaction disruption.

claim: SOX9 homodimerization was unperturbed by Sm4 at up to 200 μM.
source: Importantly, neither SOX7 nor SOX17 have the capacity to form a homodimer, and thus this component of Sm4 mode of action is highly specific to SOX18-SOX18 interaction. Further corroborating this, SOX9 homodimerization was unperturbed by Sm4 at up to 200 mM (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing lack of effect of Sm4 on SOX9 homodimerization at concentrations up to 200 μM.

claim: The most common binding motif identified from the SOX18 ChIP-seq peaks corresponds to the SOX motif 5'-AACAAT-3'.
source: The most common binding motif identified from the SOX18 ChIP-seq peaks corresponds to the previously reported SOX motif 5'-AACAAT-3' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis and references a previously reported motif.

claim: SOX18 peaks are 3.6 fold closer to the TSS of Sm4 down-regulated genes than to randomly distributed TSSs (p-value <0.001).
source: The cumulative SOX18 peak-to-TSS distance demonstrated that, overall, SOX18 peaks are 3.6 fold closer (p-value <0.001) to the TSS of Sm4 down-regulated genes than to randomly distributed TSSs (Figure 2B, top left).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing significant proximity of SOX18 binding to Sm4-affected genes.

claim: Analysis of known motifs in SOX18 ChIP-seq peaks revealed an over-representation of c-JUN binding motifs (3.23% of SOX18 peaks, p-value = 1e-302).
source: Indeed, analysis of known motifs in SOX18 ChIP-seq peaks revealed an over-representation of c-JUN binding motifs (3.23% of SOX18 peaks, p-value = 1e-302)
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis of ChIP-seq data with statistical significance.

claim: SOX18 and c-JUN can physically interact.
source: Indeed, analysis of known motifs in SOX18 ChIP-seq peaks revealed an over-representation of c-JUN binding motifs (3.23% of SOX18 peaks, p-value = 1e-302) and ALPHA-Screen analysis further established that SOX18 and c-JUN could physically interact (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data demonstrating physical interaction.

claim: Sm4 did not affect the transcriptional activity of either SOX17 or SOX9 proteins at any tested concentration (<50 μM) in cell-based reporter assays.
source: Sm4 did not affect the transcriptional activity of either SOX17 or SOX9 proteins at any tested concentration (<50 p,M) in cell-based reporter assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Robinson et al., 2014; Lefebvre et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-based reporter assay data and references to published methods.

claim: Sm4 treatment significantly reduced SOX18-dependent egfp transcript levels by 61% in zebrafish larvae.
source: We treated these larvae at 20 hr post fertilization (hpf) and observed that Sm4 treatment significantly reduced SOX18-dependent egfp transcript levels (61%), similar to the effects of combined sox7/18 depletion using morpholino oligonucleotides (MO) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from zebrafish experiments showing reduction in transcript levels.

claim: Zebrafish embryos treated with Sm4 developed normally with no evidence of toxicity.
source: Importantly, these zebrafish embryos developed normally and we found no evidence of toxicity.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data from zebrafish experiments.

claim: When rbpj MO injections at suboptimal dose were combined with Sm4 treatment, the repressive effect was significantly increased by 11.5%.
source: In addition, when rbpj MO injections at suboptimal dose were combined with Sm4 treatment, the repressive effect was significantly increased by 11.5% (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from zebrafish reporter assays showing synergistic effect.

claim: Continuous Sm4 treatment between 2 and 6 days post fertilization did not perturb the transcriptional activity of Sox9 or the process of chondrogenesis in zebrafish.
source: As a negative control in vivo, we used the Sox9-dependent tg(col2a1:yfp) reporter line, and observed that continuous Sm4 treatment between 2 and 6 days post fertilization did not perturb the transcriptional activity of Sox9 or the process of chondrogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo zebrafish reporter data demonstrating selectivity of Sm4.

claim: Zebrafish larvae treated with 1.5 μM Sm4 acquired an enlarged posterior cardinal vein (PCV) at the expense of the dorsal aorta (DA).
source: We treated zebrafish larvae harbouring the arterial/venous reporter tg(fli1a:eGFP,—6.5kdrl:mCherry) with 1.5 pM Sm4 during the relevant developmental window, starting from 16 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A). These larvae acquired an enlarged posterior cardinal vein (PCV) at the expense of the dorsal aorta (DA) (Figure 3E–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), with arteriovenous shunts and incomplete trunk circulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and phenotypic analysis of zebrafish vascular development.

claim: qRT-PCR analysis revealed significant dysregulation of arterial and venous genes, particularly efnb2a, hey1 and efnb4a, in Sm4-treated zebrafish larvae.
source: qRT-PCR analysis of blood vascular markers at 24 and 48 hpf revealed a significant dysregulation of arterial and venous genes in Sm4-treated conditions compared to DMSO, particularly efnb2a, hey1 and efnb4a (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing differential gene expression in treated versus control zebrafish.

claim: Sm4 was consistently detected in blood plasma at two different time points, with a mean concentration increasing over time from 38.3 μg/mL to 55.2 μg/mL.
source: We next went on to measure Sm4 bioavailability during the course of the treatment. Sm4 was consistently detected in blood plasma at two different time points, with a mean concentration increasing over time from 38.3 Mg/ mL to 55.2 Mg/mL (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements of Sm4 in mouse blood plasma.

claim: Sm4-treated mice had a significant increase in their overall survival with a median latency of 44 days compared to 33 and 34 days for PBS vehicle- or aspirin-treated mice (p-value <0.01).
source: PBS vehicle- or aspirin-treated mice succumbed to the 4T1.2 tumor burden with a median latency of 33 and 34 days respectively (Figure 4D), whereas Sm4-treated mice had a significant increase in their overall survival with a median latency of 44 days (p-value <0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis data from the mouse breast cancer model with statistical significance.

claim: There was a 67% reduction in the mean number of lung metastases at day 28 after tumor inoculation in Sm4-treated mice.
source: While the size of the primary tumor was unchanged by Sm4 treatment (Figure 4E), we found a 67% reduction in the mean number of lung metastases at day 28 after tumor inoculation (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of lung metastases in the mouse model.

claim: The size of the primary tumor was unchanged by Sm4 treatment.
source: While the size of the primary tumor was unchanged by Sm4 treatment (Figure 4E), we found a 67% reduction in the mean number of lung metastases at day 28 after tumor inoculation (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor size measurements during the treatment period.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the number of endothelial cells (48%, p-value <0.05) in the tumors of Sm4-treated mice.
source: Further analysis using immunofluorescent staining for endothelial cell markers ERG (nuclear) and Endomucin (EMCN, membranous), showed a significant decrease in the number of endothelial cells (48%, p-value <0.05), as well as the volume of the blood vessels (55%, p-value <0.01) in the tumors of Sm4-treated mice (Figure 4H,I, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence analysis of tumor sections with statistical significance.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the volume of the blood vessels (55%, p-value <0.01) in the tumors of Sm4-treated mice.
source: Further analysis using immunofluorescent staining for endothelial cell markers ERG (nuclear) and Endomucin (EMCN, membranous), showed a significant decrease in the number of endothelial cells (48%, p-value <0.05), as well as the volume of the blood vessels (55%, p-value <0.01) in the tumors of Sm4-treated mice (Figure 4H,I, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence analysis of tumor sections with statistical significance.

claim: The density of the tumor associated lymphatic vessels was greatly reduced (65%, p-value <0.01) in Sm4-treated mice.
source: Using lymphatic specific markers PROX1 and podoplanin (PDPN), we also assessed the effect of Sm4 on the tumor induced lymphangiogenic response, and found that the density of the tumor associated lymphatic vessels was greatly reduced (65%, p-value <0.01) in treated conditions, as well as the number of lymphatic endothelial cells (70%, p-value <0.001) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence analysis of lymphatic vessels with statistical significance.

claim: The number of lymphatic endothelial cells was reduced (70%, p-value <0.001) in Sm4-treated mice.
source: Using lymphatic specific markers PROX1 and podoplanin (PDPN), we also assessed the effect of Sm4 on the tumor induced lymphangiogenic response, and found that the density of the tumor associated lymphatic vessels was greatly reduced (65%, p-value <0.01) in treated conditions, as well as the number of lymphatic endothelial cells (70%, p-value <0.001) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence analysis of lymphatic endothelial cells with statistical significance.

claim: The SOXF group (SOX7, SOX17 and SOX18) of transcription factors are key regulators of endothelial cell differentiation during development.
source: The SOXF group (SOX7, —17 and —18) of transcription factors (TFs) are key regulators of endothelial cell differentiation during development (François et al., 2008; Corada et al., 2013; Hosking et al., 2009; Matsui et al., 2006; Cermenati et al., 2008; Herpers et al., 2008), and are thus critical for the formation of vasculature.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: SOXF transcription factors are critical for the formation of vasculature.
source: The SOXF group (SOX7, —17 and —18) of transcription factors (TFs) are key regulators of endothelial cell differentiation during development (François et al., 2008; Corada et al., 2013; Hosking et al., 2009; Matsui et al., 2006; Cermenati et al., 2008; Herpers et al., 2008), and are thus critical for the formation of vasculature.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the role of SOXF in endothelial cell differentiation and supported by citations.

claim: Mutation or deletion of SoxF genes compromises arteriovenous specification, blood vascular integrity and lymphangiogenesis.
source: Mutation or deletion of SoxF genes compromises arteriovenous specification, blood vascular integrity and lymphangiogenesis, and inhibits tumour growth and metastasis in animal models of cancer (Duong et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2009; Young et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Mutation or deletion of SoxF genes inhibits tumour growth and metastasis in animal models of cancer.
source: Mutation or deletion of SoxF genes compromises arteriovenous specification, blood vascular integrity and lymphangiogenesis, and inhibits tumour growth and metastasis in animal models of cancer (Duong et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2009; Young et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: High levels of SOX18 have been associated with poor prognosis for cancer in human patients.
source: More recently, high levels of SOX18 have been associated with poor prognosis for cancer in human patients (Eom et al., 2012; Pula et al., 2013; Jethon et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published clinical research.

claim: SOX18 loss of function is compensated by the action of the remaining SOXF proteins.
source: Any attempt to develop pharmaceutically useful SOX18 inhibitors must overcome two obstacles — first, that SOX18 loss of function is compensated by the action of the remaining SOXF (Hosking et al., 2009), and second, that each SOXF factor is likely to have several partners that may themselves act redundantly.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: SOX proteins activate individual target genes by recruiting specific interacting partners.
source: SOX proteins activate individual target genes by recruiting specific interacting partners (Sarkar and Hochedlinger, 2013), but only two protein-protein interactions for the SOXF group (SOX18-MEF2C and SOX17-OCT4) have been identified to date (Hosking et al., 2001; Jauch et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Only two protein-protein interactions for the SOXF group (SOX18-MEF2C and SOX17-OCT4) have been identified prior to this study.
source: SOX proteins activate individual target genes by recruiting specific interacting partners (Sarkar and Hochedlinger, 2013), but only two protein-protein interactions for the SOXF group (SOX18-MEF2C and SOX17-OCT4) have been identified to date (Hosking et al., 2001; Jauch et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Sm4 is derived from a natural product found in the brown alga Caulocystis cephalornithos.
source: Sm4, derived from a natural product found in the brown alga Caulocystis cephalornithos, was identified in a high-throughput screen for potential SOX18 blockers (Fontaine et al., to be published in full elsewhere).
evidence: The claim is based on the source of the compound and references unpublished work.

claim: Sm4 was identified in a high-throughput screen for potential SOX18 blockers.
source: Sm4, derived from a natural product found in the brown alga Caulocystis cephalornithos, was identified in a high-throughput screen for potential SOX18 blockers (Fontaine et al., to be published in full elsewhere).
evidence: The claim is based on the screening method used to identify the compound and references unpublished work.

claim: SOX18 is able to interact with all endothelial transcription factors tested, with the possible exception of SOX17 and CTNNB1.
source: SOX18 was found to interact with all endothelial transcription factors tested, with the possible exception of SOX17 and CTNNB1, which showed a binding affinity below the arbitrary threshold (Figure 1C, '-').
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data.

claim: All three SOXF proteins can form a heterodimer with OCT4.
source: We further found that all three SOXF proteins can form a heterodimer with OCT4, whereas only the SOX17-OCT4 interaction is affected by Sm4.
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data.

claim: Only the SOX17-OCT4 interaction is affected by Sm4.
source: We further found that all three SOXF proteins can form a heterodimer with OCT4, whereas only the SOX17-OCT4 interaction is affected by Sm4.
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data showing selective disruption.

claim: Neither SOX7 nor SOX17 have the capacity to form a homodimer.
source: Importantly, neither SOX7 nor SOX17 have the capacity to form a homodimer, and thus this component of Sm4 mode of action is highly specific to SOX18-SOX18 interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data showing lack of homodimerization.

claim: The homodimerization disruption component of Sm4 mode of action is highly specific to SOX18-SOX18 interaction.
source: Importantly, neither SOX7 nor SOX17 have the capacity to form a homodimer, and thus this component of Sm4 mode of action is highly specific to SOX18-SOX18 interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that only SOX18 forms homodimers among SOXF proteins.

claim: Sm4 selectivity leans towards a subset of SOX18-associated PPIs, but has the capability to interfere with SOX7 or SOX17 protein partner recruitment.
source: These results show that Sm4 selectivity leans towards a subset of SOX18-associated PPIs, but has the capability to interfere with SOX7 or SOX17 protein partner recruitment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ALPHA-Screen data showing effects on multiple SOXF proteins.

claim: The capability of Sm4 to interfere with SOX7 or SOX17 protein partner recruitment is potentially advantageous in preventing SOXF redundancy mechanism.
source: This feature of Sm4 is potentially advantageous in preventing SOXF redundancy mechanism (Hosking et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the therapeutic advantage, supported by citations about SOXF redundancy.

claim: Known SOX18 target genes include Prox1 and Vcam1.
source: The validity of this ChIP- seq dataset was further confirmed by GO term analysis and identification of known SOX18 target genes such as Proxl and Vcaml (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; François et al., 2008; Hosking et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data and citations to published research.

claim: Sm4 does not have an off-target effect on the transcriptional activity of 7 other transcription factors tested (cMYC, GATA2, c-FOS, c-JUN, CTCF, EZH2, MAX).
source: This correlation was not observed for 7 of the other transcription factors tested (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, Supplementary file 1c), signifying that Sm4 does not have an off-target effect on these TFs activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of correlation between Sm4-affected genes and binding sites of other TFs.

claim: The expression levels of the other TFs tested were unaltered by Sm4 treatment.
source: We found that the expression levels of the other TFs tested were unaltered by Sm4 treatment (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing no change in TF expression levels.

claim: Sm4 selectively targets SOX18-mediated transcription over other key endothelial transcription factors and SOX proteins.
source: Together, these results provide strong evidence that Sm4 selectively targets SOX18-mediated transcription over other key endothelial transcription factors and SOX proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and reporter assays.

claim: The tg(-6.5kdrl:eGFP) transgenic zebrafish reporter line was previously validated as a readout for the combined activity of Sox7 and Sox18.
source: To investigate whether Sm4 is also able to perturb Sox18 transcriptional activation in vivo, we used the tg(−6.5kdrl:eGFP) transgenic zebrafish reporter line, previously validated as a readout for the combined activity of Sox7 and Sox18 (Duong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published validation of the reporter line.

claim: Sm4 interferes with Sox7/18 and Rbpj co-ordinated activation of the Dll4in3 enhancer.
source: These data show that Sm4 interferes with Sox7/18 and Rbpjco-ordinated activation of the Dll4in3 enhancer.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the reporter assay data showing effects of Sm4 on Dll4in3:eGFP expression.

claim: The hallmark of sox7 genetic disruption is a short circulatory loop in the head formed by the lateral dorsal artery.
source: The hallmark of sox7 genetic disruption is a short circulatory loop in the head formed by the lateral dorsal artery (Mohammed et al., 2013), resulting in perturbed facial circulation (Hermkens et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on sox7 phenotypes.

claim: Sox7 genetic disruption results in perturbed facial circulation.
source: The hallmark of sox7 genetic disruption is a short circulatory loop in the head formed by the lateral dorsal artery (Mohammed et al., 2013), resulting in perturbed facial circulation (Hermkens et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research on sox7 phenotypes.

claim: Sox7 activity is only partially affected in presence of Sm4.
source: However, the blood circulation in the head is unaffected in Sm4-treated larvae, signifying that a short circulatory loop has not fully formed. This phenotype supports of the conclusion that Sox7 activity is only partially affected in presence of the small compound.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Sm4-treated larvae do not show the full sox7 loss-of-function phenotype.

claim: Sm4 selectively interfered with the transcriptional activity of Sox18 and SoxF-mediated vascular formation in vivo.
source: Overall, these results are congruent with the genome-wide inhibitory effects observed in vitro, demonstrating that Sm4 selectively interfered with the transcriptional activity of Sox18 and SoxF-mediated vascular formation in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple in vivo zebrafish experiments showing effects on Sox18/SoxF activity.

claim: Sox18 is expressed in the 4T1.2 tumor vasculature.
source: As an indirect indication of target engagement, we first confirmed the expression of Sox18 in the 4T1.2 tumor vasculature by in situ hybridization (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing Sox18 expression in tumor vasculature.

claim: Sm4 improved the outcome of induced breast cancer by interfering with tumor-induced neo-vascularization and associated metastasis.
source: Together, this demonstrates that Sm4 improved the outcome of induced breast cancer by interfering with tumor-induced neo-vascularization and associated metastasis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple observations including reduced vascular density, reduced metastases, and improved survival.

claim: Induction of angio- and lymphangiogenesis is a hallmark of solid cancer.
source: Induction of angio- and lymphangiogenesis is a hallmark of solid cancer, and is a critical step towards enabling tumor metastatic dissemination.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: Induction of angio- and lymphangiogenesis is a critical step towards enabling tumor metastatic dissemination.
source: Induction of angio- and lymphangiogenesis is a hallmark of solid cancer, and is a critical step towards enabling tumor metastatic dissemination.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cancer metastasis.

claim: Conventional approaches to target transcription factors have focused on interfering with oncogenes that are dysregulated to promote tumor cell transformation.
source: Conventional approaches to target transcription factors have focused on interfering with oncogenes that are dysregulated to promote tumor cell transformation (Gormally et al., 2014; Illendula et al., 2015; Moellering et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on transcription factor targeting strategies.

claim: Targeting the transcription factor SOX18 with Sm4 is an effective molecular strategy to interfere with the metastatic spread in a pre-clinical model of breast cancer.
source: Our results provide a proof of concept that targeting the transcription factor SOX18 with Sm4 is an effective molecular strategy to interfere with the metastatic spread in a pre-clinical model of breast cancer.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing reduced metastasis and improved survival in the mouse model.

claim: The study validates an interactome-based molecular strategy to interfere with transcription factor activity for the development of novel disease therapeutics.
source: Our studies validate an interactome-based molecular strategy to interfere with transcription factor activity, for the development of novel disease therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the overall approach and results of the study.

claim: Pharmacological targeting of transcription factors holds great promise for the development of new therapeutics.
source: Pharmacological targeting of transcription factors holds great promise for the development of new therapeutics, but strategies based on blockade of DNA binding, nuclear shuttling, or individual protein partner recruitment have yielded limited success to date.
evidence: The claim is based on general scientific knowledge and context about transcription factor targeting.

claim: Strategies based on blockade of DNA binding, nuclear shuttling, or individual protein partner recruitment have yielded limited success to date.
source: Pharmacological targeting of transcription factors holds great promise for the development of new therapeutics, but strategies based on blockade of DNA binding, nuclear shuttling, or individual protein partner recruitment have yielded limited success to date.
evidence: The claim is based on general scientific knowledge about limitations of current transcription factor targeting approaches.

claim: Transcription factors typically engage in complex interaction networks, likely masking the effects of specifically inhibiting single protein-protein interactions.
source: Transcription factors typically engage in complex interaction networks, likely masking the effects of specifically inhibiting single protein-protein interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on general scientific knowledge and speculation about why single PPI inhibition has limited success.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of SOX18 protein function presents a potential avenue for management of the vascular response in cancer.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of SOX18 protein function therefore presents a potential avenue for management of the vascular response in cancer.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the role of SOX18 in vascular development and cancer.

claim: Transcription factors often operate in mutually redundant families, thwarting conventional approaches to developing transcription factor-based therapies.
source: Transcription factors often operate in mutually redundant families, thwarting conventional approaches to developing transcription factor-based therapies.
evidence: The claim is based on general scientific knowledge about transcription factor families.

claim: Each SOXF factor is likely to have several partners that may themselves act redundantly.
source: Any attempt to develop pharmaceutically useful SOX18 inhibitors must overcome two obstacles — first, that SOX18 loss of function is compensated by the action of the remaining SOXF (Hosking et al., 2009), and second, that each SOXF factor is likely to have several partners that may themselves act redundantly.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about SOXF protein partners based on general knowledge of transcription factor function.

claim: The lack of inhibition of Sm4 on the primary tumor growth suggests that a potential combined effect between the drug treatment and surgery-induced inflammation is unlikely to be responsible for the increased survival.
source: The lack of inhibition of Sm4 on the primary tumor growth (Figure 4E) suggests that a potential combined effect between the drug treatment and surgery-induced inflammation is unlikely to be responsible for the increased survival, given that surgery is required on day 0 to inoculate the xenograft cancer cells into the mammary fat pad.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that primary tumor size was unchanged.

claim: The lymphatic response to Sm4-treatment is consistent with that of SOX18 loss of function during lymphatic spread of solid cancers.
source: This lymphatic response to Sm4-treatment is consistent with that of SOX18 loss of function during lymphatic spread of solid cancers (Duong et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with published research on SOX18 loss of function.

claim: The TSS of Sm4 down-regulated genes were 2.05 fold closer to c-JUN binding events (p-value = 0.011).
source: Interestingly, the TSS of Sm4 down-regulated genes were 2.05 fold closer to c-JUN binding events (p-value = 0.011, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: The proximity of Sm4 down-regulated genes to c-JUN binding events could suggest possible co-regulation by SOX18 and c-JUN on this subset of genes.
source: Although only mildly significant, this could suggest possible co-regulation by SOX18 and c-JUN on this subset of Sm4 down-regulated genes.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the proximity analysis.

claim: The activity of the Dll4in3 enhancer does not fully recapitulate the endogenous dll4 expression.
source: The activity of this Dll4in3 enhancer does not fully recapitulate the endogenous dll4 expression (Wythe et al., 2013; Sacilotto et al., 2013), but it does provide a useful tool to study the combinatorial activity of Sox7, Sox18 and the Notch effector Rbpj.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published characterization of the reporter.

claim: The Dll4in3 enhancer provides a useful tool to study the combinatorial activity of Sox7, Sox18 and the Notch effector Rbpj.
source: The activity of this Dll4in3 enhancer does not fully recapitulate the endogenous dll4 expression (Wythe et al., 2013; Sacilotto et al., 2013), but it does provide a useful tool to study the combinatorial activity of Sox7, Sox18 and the Notch effector Rbpj.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published characterization of the reporter.

claim: Combined genetic interference with sox7, sox18 and rbpj abolishes Dll4in3 activation.
source: Combined genetic interference with sox7, sox18 and rbpj has been shown to abolish Dll4in3 activation, while single or double MO knockdowns have a much milder effect (Sacilotto et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Single or double MO knockdowns of sox7, sox18 and rbpj have a much milder effect on Dll4in3 activation than triple knockdown.
source: Combined genetic interference with sox7, sox18 and rbpj has been shown to abolish Dll4in3 activation, while single or double MO knockdowns have a much milder effect (Sacilotto et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The mild repressive effect of single or double knockdowns on Dll4in3 was recapitulated by treatment with Sm4 alone.
source: This mild repressive effect was recapitulated by treatment with Sm4 alone (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the zebrafish reporter assay.

claim: The arteriovenous specification defect phenotype is typically only observed in double loss of Sox7 and Sox18 function due to SoxF redundancy.
source: Due to SoxF redundancy in arteriovenous specification, an A/V malformation phenotype is typically only observed in double loss of Sox7 and Sox18 function.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about SoxF redundancy.

claim: SOX7 like SOX18 is able to interact with RBPJ.
source: Like SOX18, SOX7 is able to interact with RBPJ and SOX18 itself, both of which interactions are at least partially disrupted by Sm4.
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data.

claim: SOX7 is able to interact with SOX18.
source: Like SOX18, SOX7 is able to interact with RBPJ and SOX18 itself, both of which interactions are at least partially disrupted by Sm4.
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data.

claim: Both SOX7-RBPJ and SOX7-SOX18 interactions are at least partially disrupted by Sm4.
source: Like SOX18, SOX7 is able to interact with RBPJ and SOX18 itself, both of which interactions are at least partially disrupted by Sm4.
evidence: The claim is supported by ALPHA-Screen experimental data.
